25	Our audit reviewed five positions at the Austin headquarters. This memorandum focuses on the Marketing Coordinator role, which is the only position among the five that requires reclassification. The remaining four positions --- Senior Financial Analyst, Regional Sales Manager, IT Systems Administrator, and Human Resources Business Partner --- are properly classified as exempt and are not addressed in further detail here. Summary analyses of those positions have been provided to Ms. Solano under separate cover.
26	
27	**Key Finding.** The Marketing Coordinator role is currently classified as exempt under the FLSA administrative exemption at an annual salary of \$54,000. Based on our review, this classification is incorrect and should be corrected. The primary duty of the Marketing Coordinator is production-oriented work --- specifically, creating marketing collateral pursuant to detailed instructions, brand guidelines, and pre-approved templates --- rather than administrative work involving the exercise of discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance. Although the role involves a mix of routine production tasks and arguably creative or analytical duties, the predominant duties are execution-oriented: the Marketing Coordinator produces content and compiles data according to established procedures, rather than advising management, formulating strategy, or making independent decisions on matters of significance to the business. Because the role\'s primary duty is the production of marketing materials and standardized reports rather than the exercise of administrative judgment, the position does not satisfy the duties test for the administrative exemption and must be reclassified to non-exempt status.
28	
29	We recommend that Aldersgate implement the reclassification prospectively, effective no later than October 1, 2022, and begin tracking the reclassified employee\'s working hours through Lone Star Payroll Solutions, the Company\'s payroll processor located in San Antonio, Texas. This memorandum also provides a general FLSA exemption analysis framework for Aldersgate\'s ongoing use in evaluating future classifications, and addresses California-specific exemption requirements in light of the Company\'s planned expansion to Irvine, California.
30	
31	**[II. Scope and Methodology]{.underline}**
32	
33	The scope of this audit encompassed five positions classified as exempt under the FLSA white-collar exemptions at Aldersgate\'s Austin, Texas corporate headquarters. For each position, we undertook the following analytical steps:
34	
35	1\. **Document review.** We reviewed each position\'s written job description, the Company\'s internal compensation grid, payroll records maintained by Lone Star Payroll Solutions, and relevant organizational charts.
36	
37	2\. **Supervisor interviews.** We conducted interviews with the direct supervisor for each audited position to understand the supervisor\'s expectations for the role, the degree of oversight exercised, and the nature and frequency of independent decision-making by the incumbent.
38	
39	3\. **Observation of actual duties.** We observed the actual work performed by each incumbent over a representative period and compared actual duties to the written job descriptions. As is frequently the case, the actual duties performed did not always align precisely with the descriptions on file.
40	
41	4\. **Legal analysis.** We measured each position against the three-part test for FLSA white-collar exemptions: (a) the salary basis test, (b) the salary level test, and (c) the duties test applicable to the specific claimed exemption category.
42	
43	The federal salary threshold in effect at the time of this audit is \$684 per week, or \$35,568 annually (\$684 × 52 weeks), as established by the U.S. Department of Labor\'s 2019 final rule updating the regulations at 29 C.F.R. Part 541.
44	
45	Of the five positions reviewed, four were found to be properly classified as exempt. Only the Marketing Coordinator requires reclassification, as detailed in Section III below.
46	
47	This memorandum does not address the manufacturing and warehouse positions at Aldersgate\'s Seguin, Texas production facility (800 Industrial Parkway, Seguin, TX 78155). All positions at that facility are currently classified as non-exempt, and we understand that classification is not in dispute.
48	
49	**[III. Analysis of the Marketing Coordinator Role]{.underline}**
50	
51	**[A. Position Overview]{.underline}**
52	
53	The Marketing Coordinator at Aldersgate\'s Austin headquarters is currently classified as exempt under the FLSA administrative exemption. The position carries an annual salary of \$54,000 and reports directly to the Director of Marketing. The Marketing Coordinator has no supervisory responsibilities and does not direct the work of any other Aldersgate employees. The incumbent holds no hiring, firing, or disciplinary authority.
54	
55	Based on our observation of actual duties performed --- as distinct from the duties reflected in the written job description --- the Marketing Coordinator\'s working time is allocated approximately as follows:
56	
57	> • **Approximately 45% of working time** is devoted to creating marketing collateral, including brochures, email campaign content, and social media posts. This work is performed using templates, pre-approved brand guidelines, and specific direction provided by the Director of Marketing. All work product is reviewed and approved by the Director before publication or dissemination. The Marketing Coordinator does not independently determine campaign messaging, target audiences, or publication timing.
58	>
59	> • **Approximately 20% of working time** is spent coordinating with outside vendors, including printers and photographers, on scheduling and logistics. This coordination involves confirming delivery dates, transmitting specifications, and tracking order status --- tasks that follow established procedures and vendor agreements already negotiated by the Director of Marketing.
60	>
61	> • **Approximately 20% of working time** is allocated to compiling marketing performance data from pre-built analytics dashboards (primarily within the Company\'s HubSpot and Google Analytics platforms) and preparing weekly performance reports in a standardized format prescribed by the Director of Marketing. The Marketing Coordinator extracts data from existing dashboards, populates a report template, and submits the completed report for the Director\'s review. The coordinator does not design the dashboards, select the metrics to be tracked, or independently analyze the data to formulate strategic recommendations.
62	>
63	> • **Approximately 15% of working time** is spent participating in team brainstorming sessions for upcoming campaigns, providing input on messaging concepts, and attending weekly departmental meetings. While the coordinator\'s input is welcomed, the Director of Marketing retains decision-making authority over campaign strategy, budget allocation, and creative direction.
64	
65	In summary, the Marketing Coordinator\'s work is predominantly production-oriented. The role\'s core function is to execute marketing tasks --- creating collateral, coordinating logistics, and compiling data --- pursuant to instructions, templates, and established procedures, with a comparatively small portion of time devoted to activities that could be characterized as discretionary or analytical.
66	
67	**[B. Salary Basis and Salary Level Tests]{.underline}**
68	
69	The Marketing Coordinator is paid on a salary basis --- that is, the incumbent receives a fixed weekly salary of \$1,038.46 (\$54,000 ÷ 52 weeks) regardless of the number of hours worked or the quality or quantity of work performed. Our review of payroll records did not identify any improper deductions that would undermine the salary basis requirement. Accordingly, the salary basis test under 29 C.F.R. § 541.602 is satisfied.
70	
71	The Marketing Coordinator\'s weekly salary of \$1,038.46 exceeds the federal salary threshold of \$684 per week (\$35,568 annually). The salary level test under 29 C.F.R. § 541.600 is therefore also satisfied.
72	
73	However, meeting the salary basis and salary level tests is a necessary but not sufficient condition for exempt classification. The duties test must independently be satisfied. As discussed below, the Marketing Coordinator does not satisfy the duties test for the administrative exemption.
74	
75	**[C. Administrative Exemption Duties Test --- Application to Marketing Coordinator]{.underline}**
76	
77	The administrative exemption requires, in addition to the salary tests, that the employee\'s primary duty meet a two-prong duties test set forth at 29 C.F.R. § 541.200:
78	
79	**Prong 1 --- The employee\'s primary duty must be the performance of office or non-manual work directly related to the management or general business operations of the employer or the employer\'s customers.**
80	
81	Marketing is, as a general matter, a function that relates to the general business operations of an employer, and employees engaged in marketing strategy, planning, and analysis may qualify under this prong. However, the inquiry does not end with the department in which the employee sits. The question is whether the *specific employee\'s primary duty* is the type of work contemplated by the administrative exemption --- advising management, planning, negotiating, representing the company on significant matters, or otherwise performing work that \"runs the business\" --- or whether the employee\'s primary duty is production work, i.e., producing the employer\'s product or service.
82	
83	Under DOL guidance and established case law, employees who create content, assemble materials, or execute tasks according to detailed instructions and templates are performing production work, even if they are employed within a department that performs an administrative function. The administrative/production distinction turns on what the individual employee actually does, not on the function of the department as a whole.
84	
85	Here, the Marketing Coordinator\'s primary duty is the production of marketing collateral --- brochures, email campaigns, social media content --- using templates and brand guidelines furnished by the Director of Marketing, with all output subject to supervisory review and approval before dissemination. The coordinator\'s remaining duties (vendor coordination per established procedures, data compilation from pre-built dashboards in a standardized report format) are similarly routine and production-oriented. These duties do not constitute \"work directly related to the management or general business operations\" of Aldersgate in the sense intended by the regulation. The Marketing Coordinator produces marketing content; the coordinator does not set marketing strategy, determine budgets, negotiate media contracts, or advise senior management on business operations.
86	
87	**Prong 2 --- The employee\'s primary duty must include the exercise of discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance.**
88	
89	The Marketing Coordinator\'s exercise of discretion is minimal. Collateral creation follows templates and brand guidelines, leaving the coordinator to make only minor aesthetic or stylistic choices within a prescribed framework. Vendor coordination follows standard operating procedures and pre-negotiated agreements. Report compilation involves extracting data from pre-built dashboards and populating a standard template --- this is data entry and formatting, not the exercise of independent judgment. Under 29 C.F.R. § 541.202, \"discretion and independent judgment\" involves the comparison and evaluation of possible courses of conduct and acting or making decisions after the various possibilities have been considered. The routine operation of pre-built software tools and the completion of standardized reporting templates do not meet this standard.
90	
91	The approximately 15% of time the Marketing Coordinator spends in brainstorming sessions involves providing input and suggestions, but the coordinator does not make or effectively recommend decisions with respect to campaigns, budgets, or strategic direction. These sessions, while involving a degree of creative participation, do not constitute the exercise of discretion and independent judgment \"with respect to matters of significance\" --- the coordinator\'s input is advisory, and final decisions rest with the Director of Marketing.
92	
93	**The fact that a role involves some analytical or creative components does not automatically render it exempt. The critical inquiry is whether the employee\'s \*primary duty\* --- the principal, main, major, or most important duty --- involves truly discretionary administrative work, or whether the role is predominantly production-oriented with incidental analytical elements.** Here, the production-oriented duties (collateral creation, vendor coordination, and report compilation) collectively account for approximately 85% of the Marketing Coordinator\'s working time. The remaining 15% --- participation in brainstorming sessions and team meetings --- does not rise to the level of discretion and independent judgment on matters of significance, and in any event is not the primary duty.
94	
95	**Conclusion.** The Marketing Coordinator does not satisfy the administrative exemption duties test. The role\'s primary duty is production-oriented, not administrative within the meaning of 29 C.F.R. § 541.200. Reclassification to non-exempt status is required.
96	
97	**[D. Other Exemptions Considered and Rejected]{.underline}**
98	
99	In the course of our analysis, we also considered whether the Marketing Coordinator might qualify for exemption under any other FLSA white-collar category:
100	
101	> • **Executive Exemption (29 C.F.R. § 541.100).** The executive exemption requires, among other things, that the employee\'s primary duty be managing the enterprise or a customarily recognized department or subdivision thereof, and that the employee customarily and regularly direct the work of at least two or more full-time employees. The Marketing Coordinator supervises no employees and has no hiring, firing, or disciplinary authority. The executive exemption is inapplicable.
102	>
103	> • **Creative Professional Exemption (29 C.F.R. § 541.302).** The creative professional exemption applies to employees whose primary duty is the performance of work requiring invention, imagination, originality, or talent in a recognized field of artistic or creative endeavor. While the Marketing Coordinator creates marketing materials, this work is performed within the constraints of pre-existing templates, brand guidelines, and specific direction from the Director of Marketing. The coordinator does not exercise the level of artistic judgment or originality contemplated by the creative professional exemption. The exemption is inapplicable.
104	
105	No other exemption category applies to this role.
106	
107	**[IV. General FLSA Exemption Analysis Framework for Future Classifications]{.underline}**
108	
109	**[A. The Three-Part Test]{.underline}**
110	
111	For Aldersgate\'s future reference, the following is a concise restatement of the three requirements that must be satisfied simultaneously for any FLSA white-collar exemption (executive, administrative, or professional):
112	
113	1\. **Salary Basis Test.** The employee must be paid on a salary basis --- a predetermined, fixed amount paid each pay period, not subject to reduction based on variations in the quality or quantity of work performed. 29 C.F.R. § 541.602. Certain permissible deductions are enumerated in the regulations, but as a general rule, the salary must be guaranteed regardless of hours worked.
114	
115	2\. Salary Level Test. The employee\'s salary must meet the minimum threshold established by the Department of Labor. As of the date of this memorandum, the federal salary threshold is \$684 per week (\$35,568 per year), as set by the DOL\'s 2019 final rule. The DOL periodically proposes adjustments to this threshold, and Aldersgate should monitor pending rulemaking for any increases that may affect the Company\'s classifications.
116	
117	3\. **Duties Test.** The employee\'s primary duty must meet the specific substantive requirements of one of the recognized exemption categories: executive, administrative, professional (learned or creative), computer employee, or outside sales. Each category has its own distinct requirements, and satisfying one does not satisfy another.
118	
119	All three tests must be met simultaneously. A position that satisfies the salary tests but fails the applicable duties test is non-exempt and must be compensated accordingly, including overtime pay for hours worked in excess of forty per workweek.
120	
121	**[B. Key Analytical Principles]{.underline}**
122	
123	Based on our experience and the issues identified in this audit, we highlight the following principles for Aldersgate\'s ongoing classification practice:
124	
125	**Actual duties control, not job titles or descriptions. The FLSA classification analysis looks at the work an employee actually performs, not the title assigned to the position or the language of the job description. A job description that emphasizes analytical, strategic, or managerial duties does not control if the employee actually spends the preponderance of working time on routine, production-oriented tasks. Aldersgate should periodically verify that written descriptions reflect actual duties, and should base classification decisions on observed reality.**
126	
127	**Hybrid roles require careful scrutiny.** Many modern positions blend functions that, considered in isolation, might be exempt with functions that are clearly non-exempt. When a position involves such a blend, the classification turns on which duties constitute the employee\'s \"primary duty.\" Under federal law, the \"primary duty\" is the principal, main, major, or most important duty performed. Time spent on various duties is a relevant factor, though not necessarily dispositive. However, where the quantitative time allocation overwhelmingly favors non-exempt production work, the primary duty analysis will almost invariably reach the same conclusion.
128	
129	**Running pre-built reports and using software as an end user does not constitute \"discretion and independent judgment.\"** Under 29 C.F.R. § 541.202, the exercise of discretion and independent judgment involves comparing and evaluating possible courses of conduct, acting or making decisions after considering various possibilities, and having the authority to make independent choices free from immediate direction or supervision. Routine data extraction from pre-configured dashboards, population of standardized report templates, and end-user operation of software tools --- even sophisticated ones --- does not satisfy this standard. The fact that an employee uses analytical software does not transform routine data compilation into the exercise of discretion.
130	
131	**The production versus administrative distinction is critical.** Employees who produce the employer\'s product or deliver its services are generally non-exempt, even if they possess specialized skills or work in departments that perform administrative functions. The administrative exemption is reserved for employees who \"run the business\" --- those engaged in servicing the business itself through functions such as human resources, finance, legal, information technology strategy, compliance, and marketing *strategy* at a senior level --- rather than producing or delivering the employer\'s goods and services to its customers.
132	
133	**Reliance on external consultants does not substitute for legal analysis. While Aldersgate may appropriately engage compensation consultants and HR advisers for benchmarking, organizational design, and market analysis, an HR consultant\'s recommendation regarding FLSA classification is not legal advice and does not carry the same weight as a legal analysis grounded in the statute, regulations, and case law. Classification is ultimately a legal determination. We recommend that the Company always have counsel review a consultant\'s exemption recommendation before implementation, particularly for hybrid roles where the classification outcome is not self-evident. A consultant\'s recommendation, standing alone, is unlikely to provide a sufficient basis for a good-faith defense if the classification is later challenged.**
134	
135	**[V. California-Specific Exemption Requirements]{.underline}**
136	
137	**[A. Context]{.underline}**
138	
139	Aldersgate is currently evaluating the establishment of a satellite office at 2100 Main Street, Suite 415, Irvine, California 92614. While no positions have been created at that location as of the date of this memorandum, we provide the following framework for California wage-and-hour compliance so that Aldersgate is prepared to apply the correct legal standards when the Irvine office opens and positions are established there.
140	
141	**[B. California Salary Threshold]{.underline}**
142	
143	California imposes its own salary threshold for exempt employees that is separate from, and currently higher than, the federal threshold. Under California Labor Code § 515(a), an employee classified as exempt must earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment (defined as forty hours per week).
144	
145	The calculation methodology is as follows: California\'s applicable minimum wage is multiplied by two to yield the minimum hourly rate for exempt status, which is then multiplied by 2,080 annual hours (40 hours per week × 52 weeks) to arrive at the annual exempt salary threshold.
146	
147	As an illustration, the California minimum wage as of January 1, 2022 was \$15.00 per hour for employers with twenty-six or more employees. Applying the formula: \$15.00 × 2 = \$30.00 per hour × 2,080 hours = \$62,400 per year. An employee classified as exempt in California must therefore earn at least \$62,400 annually as of the 2022 threshold.
148	
149	**Critical Warning. California\'s minimum wage is subject to scheduled annual increases, and the exempt salary threshold rises correspondingly. Aldersgate must re-verify the applicable California exempt salary threshold at the time any California positions are established and whenever the California minimum wage changes thereafter. Failure to pay at least the California exempt salary threshold renders the employee non-exempt as a matter of California law, regardless of whether the employee\'s duties would otherwise satisfy the exemption criteria. This threshold is frequently higher than the federal threshold and has caught many employers off guard when they apply a uniform national salary structure across multiple states without accounting for California\'s heightened requirements. An employee earning \$54,000 or \$55,000 annually, for example, would meet the federal salary threshold but would fall short of California\'s exempt salary threshold, resulting in automatic non-exempt status under California law.**
150	
151	**[C. California \"Primarily Engaged\" Duties Test]{.underline}**
152	
153	In addition to its higher salary threshold, California applies a stricter duties test than the federal FLSA. Under the federal standard, the classification analysis examines the employee\'s \"primary duty\" --- a qualitative, totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry in which time spent is one relevant factor but is not necessarily determinative. California, by contrast, applies a quantitative \"primarily engaged\" standard under its Industrial Welfare Commission (\"IWC\") Wage Orders.
154	
155	Under the California standard, an employee qualifies for exempt status only if the employee is \"primarily engaged\" in duties that meet the criteria for the applicable exemption. California courts have interpreted \"primarily engaged\" to mean that the employee must spend **more than fifty percent (50%) of actual working time** performing duties that independently qualify for the exemption. This is a time-based, quantitative test --- not a qualitative balancing of the relative importance of various duties.
156	
157	The practical consequence of this standard is significant. If an employee spends fifty percent or less of working time on genuinely exempt duties, the employee is non-exempt under California law, even if the same employee would qualify as exempt under the federal FLSA. Any hybrid role that blends routine, production-oriented, or scripted tasks with exempt-qualifying duties must be carefully time-studied before an exempt classification is assigned in California. Roles in which routine or production-oriented tasks consume fifty percent or more of the workday will not qualify for exemption under California law, regardless of how the duties test analysis would come out under the federal standard. See California Labor Code § 515(a); IWC Wage Orders.
158	
159	**[VI. Willfulness, Liquidated Damages, and the Consequences of Misclassification]{.underline}**
160	
161	**[A. Federal FLSA Exposure]{.underline}**
162	
163	Misclassification of an employee as exempt under the FLSA exposes the employer to the following categories of liability:
164	
165	**Back Pay.** Employees misclassified as exempt are entitled to recover unpaid overtime compensation for all hours worked in excess of forty in any workweek, calculated at one and one-half times their regular rate of pay. 29 U.S.C. § 207(a). The regular rate is derived from the employee\'s actual compensation for the workweek in question.
166	
167	**Statute of Limitations.** The standard FLSA statute of limitations for recovery of unpaid wages is two years from the date of each violation. 29 U.S.C. § 255(a). However, for **willful** violations, the statute of limitations is extended to **three years**. *Id.* The distinction between a two-year and a three-year limitations period can materially increase the total exposure, particularly where the misclassification has been ongoing for an extended period.
168	
169	**Liquidated Damages.** Under 29 U.S.C. § 216(b), an employee who prevails on an FLSA overtime claim may recover liquidated damages in an amount equal to the unpaid overtime --- effectively doubling the back-pay recovery. Liquidated damages are mandatory unless the employer demonstrates that it acted in good faith and had reasonable grounds to believe that its classification of the employee was lawful. This is a difficult burden for the employer to carry.
170	
171	**Attorneys\' Fees and Costs.** A prevailing employee is entitled to an award of reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs of the action. 29 U.S.C. § 216(b). Fee awards can be substantial in FLSA litigation.
172	
173	**[B. The \"Willfulness\" Standard and Its Implications for Aldersgate]{.underline}**
174	
175	A violation of the FLSA is \"willful\" if the employer either knew that its conduct was prohibited by the statute or showed reckless disregard for whether its conduct violated the statute. *McLaughlin v. Richland Shoe Co.*, 486 U.S. 128, 133 (1988). Reckless disregard does not require proof that the employer acted with malicious intent; rather, it is sufficient to show that the employer failed to make adequate inquiry into whether its conduct was lawful, or that the employer disregarded information indicating that its conduct violated the law.
176	
177	**We strongly advise Aldersgate that in any future classification decision, if counsel identifies a significant risk that a role does not meet the requirements for exempt status, proceeding with an exempt classification over that advice could support a finding of willfulness. This is true even if the employer has received a contrary recommendation from an HR consultant or compensation adviser. Legal classification is a question of law, and an employer that privileges a consultant\'s recommendation over counsel\'s legal analysis does so at the risk of demonstrating the very \"reckless disregard\" that triggers the three-year statute of limitations and mandatory liquidated damages. A consultant\'s market-based or organizational-design recommendation, however well-intentioned, is not a substitute for legal analysis, and reliance on such a recommendation does not establish the \"reasonable grounds\" necessary to defeat a liquidated damages claim when contrary legal advice has been received.**
178	
179	The receipt of legal advice identifying a classification risk creates a record. If an employer is later shown to have received counsel\'s analysis concluding that a role likely does not qualify for exempt status, yet proceeded to classify the role as exempt based on a different recommendation from a non-legal source, a court is likely to find that the employer acted with knowledge of the risk or, at minimum, with reckless disregard for whether the classification violated the FLSA. Such a finding would extend the statute of limitations from two years to three years and would effectively preclude the employer from avoiding liquidated damages.
180	
181	The willfulness risk is particularly acute in multi-employee contexts. When the same misclassification is applied to a class of similarly situated employees --- for example, where a role is filled by multiple incumbents at various office locations --- the extended three-year limitations period and mandatory liquidated damages multiply across every affected employee. What might be a manageable back-pay exposure for a single employee can become a significant liability when applied across a group.
182	
183	We therefore urge Aldersgate to treat counsel\'s classification analysis as the controlling input in any exemption decision, particularly for hybrid roles where the outcome is not clear-cut. If counsel and a consultant disagree on whether a role qualifies for exempt status, the conservative course --- and the course most protective of the Company --- is to follow counsel\'s recommendation, classify the role as non-exempt, and implement appropriate timekeeping procedures. The incremental administrative cost of tracking hours for a non-exempt employee is trivial compared to the potential exposure from a misclassification claim compounded by a willfulness finding.
184	
185	**[C. California-Specific Penalties]{.underline}**
186	
187	If Aldersgate establishes positions in California that are later found to have been misclassified, California law provides additional penalties and remedies beyond those available under the federal FLSA:
188	
189	**Waiting Time Penalties.** Under California Labor Code § 203, an employer that willfully fails to pay all wages due to an employee at the time of termination (including overtime that should have been paid) may be assessed a penalty of up to thirty days\' wages at the employee\'s daily rate of pay. For a misclassified exempt employee who separates from employment with unpaid overtime owing, this penalty can add a substantial sum to the total exposure.
190	
191	**Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA).** California Labor Code § 2698 *et seq.* authorizes aggrieved employees to bring representative actions on behalf of themselves and other current and former employees for violations of the California Labor Code. PAGA penalties are \$100 per employee per pay period for initial violations and \$200 per employee per pay period for subsequent violations. Seventy-five percent of PAGA penalties are payable to the State of California through the Labor and Workforce Development Agency, and twenty-five percent are retained by the aggrieved employees. PAGA claims cannot be waived through pre-dispute arbitration agreements and can result in significant aggregate exposure, particularly where the violation affects multiple employees over an extended period.
192	
193	**California Overtime Calculation.** California requires overtime pay not only for hours worked in excess of forty in a workweek (consistent with federal law) but also for hours worked in excess of eight in a single workday and for hours worked on the seventh consecutive day in a workweek. Double-time pay is required for hours worked in excess of twelve in a single day. These daily overtime requirements can significantly increase back-pay exposure compared to the federal calculation, particularly for employees who occasionally work long days even if their weekly total does not substantially exceed forty hours.
194	
195	**[VII. Recommendations]{.underline}**
196	
197	**[A. Immediate Actions]{.underline}**
198	
199	Based on the analysis set forth above, we recommend the following immediate steps:
200	
201	1\. **Reclassify the Marketing Coordinator to non-exempt status** effective no later than October 1, 2022. Coordinate with Lone Star Payroll Solutions to transition the position from salaried-exempt to hourly non-exempt compensation. The recommended hourly rate is \$26.00 per hour, which is approximately equivalent to the current \$54,000 annual salary on a forty-hour workweek basis (\$54,000 ÷ 2,080 hours = \$25.96/hour, rounded to \$26.00).
202	
203	2\. **Implement time tracking** for the reclassified Marketing Coordinator position through Lone Star Payroll Solutions\' electronic timekeeping platform. The employee must record all hours worked, including any time worked before or after regular business hours and during meal periods.
204	
205	3\. **Conduct a communication with the affected employee** explaining that the reclassification is a compliance measure undertaken to ensure proper application of federal wage-and-hour law. The communication should make clear that the reclassification is not a demotion, a reduction in compensation, or an adverse employment action of any kind.
206	
207	4\. **Assess back-pay exposure.** Based on our review, the Marketing Coordinator has rarely worked more than forty-two hours in any workweek, which limits the total unpaid overtime exposure. We recommend a voluntary self-audit for the two-year lookback period (September 2020 through September 2022) to quantify any overtime owed and to make the employee whole proactively. A voluntary correction will support a good-faith defense against any future claim for liquidated damages and will mitigate the risk that the misclassification is characterized as willful.
208	
209	**[B. Ongoing Compliance Measures]{.underline}**
210	
211	1\. **Future classifications of hybrid roles.** Any new position or restructured role that blends routine, production-oriented functions with analytical, managerial, or otherwise potentially exempt functions should be reviewed by legal counsel before an exempt classification is assigned. HR consultant recommendations, while valuable for compensation benchmarking and organizational design purposes, should be treated as one input into the classification decision --- not as dispositive. The final determination of exempt or non-exempt status is a legal question and should be made by or in consultation with counsel.
212	
213	2\. California expansion. Before establishing any exempt-classified positions at the planned Irvine, California office, Aldersgate must confirm that (a) the salary for each position meets or exceeds California\'s exempt salary threshold as calculated at the time of hire (and recalculated annually whenever the California minimum wage changes), and (b) each employee will be \"primarily engaged\" in exempt-qualifying duties for more than fifty percent of actual working time. Positions that do not satisfy both the California salary threshold and the California \"primarily engaged\" duties test must be classified as non-exempt under California law, even if they would qualify for exempt status under the federal FLSA.
214	
215	3\. Annual classification review. We recommend that Aldersgate institute an annual review of exempt classifications, with particular attention to roles whose actual duties have evolved since the original classification was assigned. Position duties often drift over time as business needs change, and a classification that was correct at inception may become incorrect as the role\'s primary duties shift.
216	
217	4\. Documentation. Aldersgate should maintain contemporaneous written documentation of the classification analysis for each exempt position, including the legal basis for the exemption determination, the factual findings supporting the duties test analysis, and the identity of the individuals who participated in the classification decision. This documentation supports a good-faith defense if the classification is subsequently challenged and demonstrates that the Company took the classification question seriously.
218	
219	**[VIII. Conclusion]{.underline}**
220	
221	Based on the analysis set forth in this memorandum, the Marketing Coordinator role at Aldersgate\'s Austin, Texas headquarters must be reclassified from exempt to non-exempt status under the FLSA. The position does not satisfy the duties test for the administrative exemption because the primary duty is production-oriented work --- the creation of marketing collateral per templates and instructions, routine vendor coordination, and standardized data compilation --- rather than the exercise of discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance.
222	
223	The remaining four positions reviewed in this audit --- Senior Financial Analyst, Regional Sales Manager, IT Systems Administrator, and Human Resources Business Partner --- are properly classified as exempt and do not require reclassification at this time.
224	
225	Aldersgate should adopt the ongoing compliance measures recommended in Section VII above, with particular attention to the classification of hybrid roles and the California-specific requirements that will apply to any positions established at the planned Irvine office. Natalie Sung and the Ridgewater & Calloway employment law team remain available to assist with any future classification questions, including the analysis of positions to be created in California or elsewhere.

**[II. Background: Role Overview and Restructuring Context]{.underline}**

As part of Aldersgate\'s January 2025 restructuring of the Customer Experience Division, two legacy positions were eliminated: the Customer Insights Analyst, which had been classified as exempt and salaried at \$72,000 per year, and the Senior Customer Service Representative, which had been classified as non-exempt and paid hourly at a rate of \$24.50 per hour. The CEAS role is designed to combine functions from both of these eliminated positions into a single hybrid role within the Customer Experience Division. By consolidating analytical and customer-facing responsibilities into a unified position, Aldersgate seeks to improve operational efficiency and reduce headcount costs while maintaining the quality of customer experience delivery and data-driven decision-making.

The CEAS role reports to a Customer Experience Team Lead, who in turn reports to the Customer Experience Manager, who reports directly to you as Vice President of Customer Experience. Internally, the position is classified at Grade 7 on Aldersgate\'s compensation scale. The corresponding salary band for Grade 7 positions ranges from \$50,000 to \$62,000 annually.

According to the February 10, 2025 job description, the CEAS role\'s duties are allocated as follows:

> • **Customer Service and Complaint Resolution** --- 40% of time: Responding to inbound customer inquiries, processing complaints, managing escalation workflows, and ensuring timely resolution of customer issues through the Company\'s Salesforce-based CRM platform.
>
> • **Data Entry and CRM Maintenance** --- 20% of time: Entering customer interaction data, maintaining accurate records in Salesforce, updating account information, and ensuring data integrity across customer-facing systems.
>
> • **Data Analysis and Reporting** --- 25% of time: Analyzing customer satisfaction data, generating reports using Tableau and pre-built Salesforce reporting templates, identifying trends in complaint volume and product feedback, and preparing monthly trend reports for management review.
>
> • **Sales Support and Upselling** --- 15% of time: Identifying opportunities during customer interactions to promote complementary products and services, supporting seasonal promotional campaigns, and assisting the sales team with lead qualification activities.

The educational requirements for the role include a bachelor\'s degree, which is preferred but not required. A minimum of two (2) years of customer service experience is required, and proficiency in Tableau is strongly preferred. No professional certifications or advanced degrees are required for the position.

**[III. Compensation Benchmarking Analysis]{.underline}**

Thornbury conducted a compensation survey of comparable roles across three industry segments: (1) the outdoor living and home furnishings industry, (2) the retail and e-commerce sector, and (3) general consumer products companies. Our survey was limited to companies with annual revenues between \$100 million and \$300 million, consistent with Aldersgate\'s current revenue profile, in order to ensure comparability of organizational scale and compensation philosophy. Within these parameters, Thornbury surveyed positions with titles including \"Customer Experience Analyst,\" \"Customer Insights Specialist,\" \"CX Data Analyst,\" and \"Client Services Analyst,\" among other comparable titles reflecting a similar blend of analytical and customer-facing responsibilities.

The results of our benchmarking analysis are summarized below:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Percentile**          **Annual Salary**       **Weekly Equivalent**
  ----------------------- ----------------------- -----------------------
  25th                    \$48,000                \$923.08

  45th (CEAS Proposed)    \$55,200                \$1,061.54

  50th (Median)           \$58,500                \$1,125.00

  75th                    \$69,000                \$1,326.92
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The proposed annual salary for the CEAS role is \$55,200, which translates to \$1,061.54 per week or approximately \$26.54 per hour based on a standard forty (40) hour workweek. This proposed salary places the CEAS role at approximately the **45th percentile** of comparable positions identified in our benchmarking study, slightly below the survey median of \$58,500 but comfortably within the competitive range.

While the proposed salary falls modestly below the market median, it is consistent with Aldersgate\'s Grade 7 compensation band (\$50,000--\$62,000) and reflects a reasonable starting point for a newly created role with no incumbent performance history. The proposed compensation is structured as a flat annual salary with no commission, bonus, or variable pay component. Thornbury recommends that Aldersgate revisit the compensation for the CEAS role within twelve to eighteen months as the position matures and actual duties, performance expectations, and market conditions become more clearly defined. At that time, an adjustment toward the 50th percentile or higher may be warranted to maintain competitive positioning in the labor market, particularly given the Tableau proficiency requirements and the hybrid nature of the role.

**[IV. Federal FLSA Salary Basis Test Analysis]{.underline}**

The FLSA\'s \"white collar\" exemptions from minimum wage and overtime requirements --- including the administrative, executive, and professional exemptions --- require, as a threshold matter, that the employee be compensated on a salary basis at a rate not less than the minimum weekly threshold established by the Department of Labor (\"DOL\"). Under the DOL\'s 2024 final rule, *Defining and Delimiting the Exemptions for Executive, Administrative, Professional, Outside Sales, and Computer Employees*, 89 Fed. Reg. 32842 (Apr. 26, 2024), the minimum weekly salary for exempt status was established at \$844 per week (\$43,888 per year), effective July 1, 2024.¹

The proposed CEAS salary of \$55,200 per year (\$1,061.54 per week) exceeds the \$844 per week salary threshold by a margin of \$217.54 per week, or approximately \$11,312 on an annualized basis. Accordingly, the proposed salary comfortably satisfies the salary basis requirement for exempt classification.

We note that, notwithstanding pending litigation regarding the 2024 rule --- specifically *State of Texas v. United States Department of Labor*, No. 4:24-cv-00499 (E.D. Tex. Nov. 15, 2024), in which the Eastern District of Texas has addressed the validity of the DOL\'s updated salary thresholds --- the proposed CEAS salary of \$55,200 per year exceeds the minimum salary threshold under any currently applicable standard. Regardless of which threshold is ultimately deemed applicable in light of ongoing legal developments, the CEAS role\'s proposed compensation is well in excess of the salary basis floor and there is no risk of failing to meet this requirement at the currently proposed salary level.

¹ The DOL\'s 2024 final rule also established a further increase to \$1,128 per week (\$58,656 per year) effective January 1, 2025, and introduced a mechanism for automatic triennial updates. These provisions have been subject to legal challenge. See *State of Texas v. U.S. Dep\'t of Labor*, No. 4:24-cv-00499 (E.D. Tex.).

**[V. Federal FLSA Administrative Exemption --- Duties Test Analysis]{.underline}**

In addition to satisfying the salary basis requirement, an employee must meet the applicable duties test in order to qualify for a white collar exemption. Thornbury has analyzed the CEAS role under the duties test for the **administrative exemption** set forth in 29 C.F.R. § 541.200, which requires that:

> \(1\) the employee\'s primary duty must be the performance of office or non-manual work directly related to the management or general business operations of the employer or the employer\'s customers; **and**
>
> \(2\) the employee\'s primary duty must include the exercise of discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance.

We address each prong in turn.

**Prong 1: Office or Non-Manual Work Directly Related to Management or General Business Operations**

The regulations at 29 C.F.R. § 541.201 provide that work \"directly related to the management or general business operations\" includes work in functional areas such as quality control, advertising, marketing, research, planning, business analysis, and similar areas that service the operational needs of the business. Thornbury concludes that the CEAS role involves work directly related to the management and general business operations of Aldersgate Outdoor Living, Inc.

The core value-add of the CEAS position lies in its data analysis and reporting function. The CEAS employee is responsible for analyzing customer satisfaction data across multiple product lines and service channels, designing and building custom Tableau dashboards to surface actionable insights, and preparing monthly trend reports that are shared directly with senior leadership and utilized in business planning and strategic decision-making. These analytical functions relate directly to Aldersgate\'s business operations planning, quality control assessment, and customer experience strategy. The CEAS employee\'s identification of patterns in product complaints directly informs Aldersgate\'s product development roadmap and influences decisions regarding product design modifications, warranty policy adjustments, and service delivery improvements. This is precisely the type of work that the administrative exemption was designed to encompass --- it services the business by providing analytical intelligence that supports management-level decision-making.

Thornbury acknowledges that the customer service and complaint resolution component constitutes approximately 40% of the CEAS role\'s time allocation. However, we view this component as incidental to the core analytical mission of the position. The direct customer interactions serve as the primary data collection mechanism for the CEAS employee\'s analytical work; the customer service function and the analytical function are integrated rather than separate, with customer-facing duties providing the raw observational data that fuels the reporting and insight generation that define the role\'s strategic contribution to the organization. Accordingly, we find that the customer service component does not undermine the administrative character of the role when the position is viewed as an integrated whole.

**Prong 2: Exercise of Discretion and Independent Judgment with Respect to Matters of Significance**

The second prong of the administrative exemption duties test requires that the employee\'s primary duty include the exercise of discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance. Under 29 C.F.R. § 541.202, the exercise of discretion and independent judgment involves the comparison and evaluation of possible courses of conduct, and acting or making a decision after the various possibilities have been considered. Factors to consider include whether the employee has authority to formulate, affect, interpret, or implement management policies or operating practices, and whether the employee carries out major assignments in conducting the operations of the business.

Thornbury concludes that the CEAS role satisfies this requirement based on the following considerations:

> \(a\) Strategic Analytical Work. The CEAS employee independently identifies patterns and trends in product complaint data to inform product development. This is strategic analytical work that directly influences Aldersgate\'s product roadmap and quality assurance priorities. The employee exercises judgment in determining which trends are significant enough to escalate and in framing the narrative presentation of data insights for senior leadership consumption.
>
> \(b\) **Dashboard Design and Visualization.** The CEAS employee designs and builds custom Tableau dashboards to surface actionable business insights. The selection of metrics, the design of visual presentations, and the determination of which data points to highlight require the exercise of independent analytical judgment that goes beyond routine data processing.
>
> \(c\) Monthly Trend Reporting. The CEAS employee prepares monthly trend reports that are distributed to senior leadership and incorporated into Aldersgate\'s business planning processes. The employee exercises discretion in structuring these reports, identifying the most significant findings, and formulating recommendations for operational improvement.
>
> \(d\) **Escalated Complaint Resolution.** The CEAS employee makes judgment calls on escalated customer complaints that go beyond the Tier 1 scripted protocols, requiring the employee to assess the circumstances of complex customer situations, evaluate the appropriate resolution, and exercise independent judgment regarding exceptions and accommodations.

Taken together, these duties demonstrate that the CEAS role involves the regular exercise of discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance to Aldersgate\'s business operations. The employee is not merely executing routine tasks under close supervision but is instead making substantive analytical contributions that inform business strategy and operational decision-making.

**[VI. Classification Recommendation]{.underline}**

Based on the foregoing analysis, Thornbury Consulting Group recommends that the Customer Experience & Analytics Specialist (\"CEAS\") role be classified as **Exempt --- Administrative** under the Fair Labor Standards Act, 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1), and the implementing regulations at 29 C.F.R. Part 541.

The CEAS role, as described in the February 10, 2025 job description, satisfies both the salary basis test and the duties test for the administrative exemption under 29 C.F.R. § 541.200. We recommend that Aldersgate designate the CEAS position as exempt on all internal payroll records and that the position be coded as \"Exempt --- Administrative\" in the Company\'s HRIS system for purposes of payroll processing, benefits administration, and regulatory reporting.

This classification recommendation applies to the CEAS role as described in the February 10, 2025 job description provided to Thornbury. If the duties allocation, reporting structure, or scope of responsibilities change materially from the job description as written, Thornbury recommends that the Company conduct a re-evaluation of the classification determination to ensure continued compliance.

**[VII. Additional Considerations and Limitations]{.underline}**

Thornbury\'s analysis is based exclusively on the written job description dated February 10, 2025 and the supplemental information provided by Aldersgate management during the course of this engagement. Because the CEAS role is newly created and no employees have yet been hired into the position, Thornbury has not had the opportunity to interview incumbent employees or observe actual job performance. It is well established that FLSA classification must be based on actual duties as performed, not solely on written job descriptions. Accordingly, actual day-to-day duties may differ from the allocations set forth in the job description, and Thornbury strongly recommends that Aldersgate revisit the classification determination after six to twelve months of actual CEAS operations to confirm that the exempt classification remains appropriate based on how the role is actually being performed.

Thornbury\'s analysis in this letter addresses federal FLSA requirements. Aldersgate should consult with its legal counsel regarding any additional state or local wage and hour requirements that may apply to employees in the Company\'s various locations. Certain states and municipalities maintain their own exemption tests, salary thresholds, and overtime requirements that may differ from the federal standards analyzed herein, and compliance with federal FLSA requirements does not necessarily ensure compliance with applicable state or local law.

Finally, this letter does not constitute legal advice. Thornbury Consulting Group is a human capital and compensation consulting firm, and our classification recommendation is provided as a consulting opinion based on our professional expertise. Aldersgate should have its legal counsel review this classification determination before implementation and prior to making any final payroll or benefits decisions affecting the CEAS position.

**[VIII. Closing]{.underline}**

We appreciate the opportunity to support Aldersgate Outdoor Living through this engagement and trust that this letter provides a clear and useful framework for your classification decision. Should you wish to discuss these findings in greater detail, or should you require any additional analysis, please do not hesitate to reach out to me directly. Thornbury is also available to assist with implementation activities, including updating the CEAS job description for compliance documentation purposes, configuring payroll coding, and conducting manager training sessions on exempt and non-exempt classification distinctions and proper pay practices.

We look forward to our continued work together.

Respectfully submitted,

H(1, "V. Federal Analysis (FLSA)")
H(2, "A. Governing Framework")
P("The FLSA requires overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek, 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1), unless an exemption applies. The administrative exemption, § 213(a)(1), requires that the employee (1) be paid on a salary basis (2) at not less than the regulatory salary level, (3) with a primary duty of office or non-manual work directly related to the management or general business operations of the employer or its customers, (4) which includes the exercise of discretion and independent judgment with respect to matters of significance. 29 C.F.R. § 541.200(a). The employer bears the burden of proving the exemption; exemptions are given a \"fair reading,\" not a narrow construction, __Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro__, 584 U.S. 79 (2018), and the employer’s burden is proof by a preponderance of the evidence, __E.M.D. Sales, Inc. v. Carrera__, 604 U.S. ___ (Jan. 15, 2025). Neither decision changes the outcome here: the problem is not the standard of construction but the facts. A job title or the employer’s label does not determine exempt status. 29 C.F.R. § 541.2.", "j")

H(2, "B. Salary Level — Satisfied, but the Record Misstates the Threshold")
P("**The operative federal threshold is $684 per week ($35,568 per year)** under the 2019 rule. The DOL’s 2024 rule (89 Fed. Reg. 32842 (Apr. 26, 2024)), which set $844/week effective July 1, 2024 and $1,128/week effective January 1, 2025, was **vacated in its entirety, nationwide**, on November 15, 2024. __State of Texas v. U.S. Dep’t of Labor__, No. 4:24-cv-00499 (E.D. Tex. Nov. 15, 2024) (consolidated with __Plano Chamber of Commerce v. U.S. Dep’t of Labor__). The DOL has enforced the 2019 levels since that ruling; any appeal should be monitored, but the $844 figure is not presently the law. The highly-compensated-employee threshold accordingly remains $107,432. The CEAS salary of $1,061.54/week exceeds $684, so the federal salary-level test is satisfied.", "j")
P("Two corrections to the record are warranted. First, Thornbury describes the case as \"pending litigation\" that \"addressed the validity\" of the thresholds, and the comp grid continues to cite the 2024 rule as operative; both are inaccurate. Second, Thornbury states there is \"no risk of failing to meet this requirement\" under \"any\" standard — but the CEAS salary ($1,061.54/week) would **not** have met the $1,128/week level the 2024 rule set for January 1, 2025. The role clears the federal floor only because that rule was vacated, and the margin would disappear under any future rulemaking at comparable levels. The Company should not design an 18-person exempt classification around a margin that thin.", "j")

H(2, "D. Duties Test — Primary Duty")
P("\"Primary duty\" means \"the principal, main, major or most important duty that the employee performs,\" determined from all the facts, with the major emphasis on the character of the employee’s job as a whole. 29 C.F.R. § 541.700(a). Relevant factors include (1) the relative importance of the exempt duties compared with other duties, (2) the amount of time spent performing exempt work, (3) the employee’s relative freedom from direct supervision, and (4) the relationship between the employee’s salary and the wages paid to other employees for the kind of nonexempt work performed by the employee. Id. Employees who spend more than 50% of their time on exempt work generally satisfy the primary-duty requirement; time is not the sole test, but it is \"a useful guide.\" § 541.700(b).", "j")

P("Thornbury’s answer to the time problem is that customer service is \"incidental\" to an \"integrated\" analytical mission because customer contacts are the \"data collection mechanism.\" That reasoning does not hold. The regulations permit nonexempt work to be disregarded only where it is directly and closely related to exempt work and the exempt work is itself the primary duty — not where the nonexempt work is the larger, independently measured, separately supervised component of the job. H(2, "E. Prong 1 — Work Directly Related to Management or General Business Operations")
P("This prong is met only by work \"directly related to assisting with the running or servicing of the business, as distinguished, for example, from working on a manufacturing production line or selling a product in a retail or service establishment.\" 29 C.F.R. § 541.201(a). Qualifying functional areas include tax, finance, accounting, quality control, purchasing, advertising, marketing, research, human resources, compliance and similar activities. § 541.201(b). Courts apply the \"administrative/production\" distinction: employees who deliver the employer’s product or service to its customers are not performing administrative work merely because the work is skilled or important. See, e.g., __Dalheim v. KDFW-TV__, 918 F.2d 1220 (5th Cir. 1990); __Bothell v. Phase Metrics, Inc.__, 299 F.3d 1120 (9th Cir. 2002); __Davis v. J.P. Morgan Chase & Co.__, 587 F.3d 529 (2d Cir. 2009); __Calderon v. GEICO Gen. Ins. Co.__, 809 F.3d 111 (4th Cir. 2015).", "j")
B("**Customer service (40%)** — answering consumer inquiries, processing returns, exchanges and warranty claims, and resolving complaints is delivery of Aldersgate’s customer service to its retail customers; it is the service the company provides, not the running of the company. The \"employer’s customers\" clause in § 541.201(c) covers employees who advise or consult with customers on the customers’ business operations (e.g., consultants), not representatives serving consumers.")
B("**CRM data entry (20%)** — recording, tabulating and updating records is classic clerical work. § 541.202(e) (clerical or secretarial work, recording or tabulating data, or performing other mechanical, repetitive, recurrent or routine work is not exempt).")
B("**Upselling (15%)** — selling the employer’s products is the paradigm the regulation excludes (\"selling a product\"). § 541.201(a).")
B("**Analytics (25%)** — customer-satisfaction and product-complaint analysis for management is closer to \"research\" or \"quality control\" and could satisfy Prong 1 in isolation. But it is only one quarter of the job.")
H(2, "F. Prong 2 — Discretion and Independent Judgment on Matters of Significance")
P("Discretion and independent judgment \"involves the comparison and the evaluation of possible courses of conduct, and acting or making a decision after the various possibilities have been considered\"; \"matters of significance\" refers to the level of importance or consequence of the work. 29 C.F.R. § 541.202(a). The § 541.202(b) factors include authority to formulate, affect, interpret or implement management policies; to commit the employer in matters with significant financial impact; to waive or deviate from established policies without prior approval; and whether the employee provides consultation or expert advice to management. It \"does not include clerical or secretarial work, recording or tabulating data, or performing other mechanical, repetitive, recurrent or routine work,\" § 541.202(e), nor does it include \"applying well-established techniques, procedures or specific standards described in manuals or other sources,\" § 541.704 (use of manuals) and § 541.202(e).", "j")
B("**Customer service:** Tier 1 and Tier 2 issues are resolved by \"scripted protocols\"; returns and warranties follow \"company policies\"; Tier 3 matters — the only ones plausibly involving significant discretion (legal complaints, social media crises, high-value retention) — are expressly **escalated** to the Manager. The CEAS has no stated authority to waive policy or grant exceptions. Thornbury’s assertion that CEAS employees make \"judgment calls on escalated customer complaints that go beyond the Tier 1 scripted protocols\" ignores that Tier 2 is also scripted and Tier 3 is escalated.")
B("**Analytics:** Dashboards are built with \"established templates and standard visualization formats\"; findings are summarized in \"standardized report formats\"; QBR work is \"as directed\"; significant NPS deviations are flagged to a non-exempt Team Lead \"for further review and action.\" This is the same pattern the 2022 audit identified as non-discretionary (\"Running pre-built reports and using software as an end user does not constitute ‘discretion and independent judgment’\"). The single aspirational sentence that the CEAS will \"proactively identify actionable insights\" does not convert templated reporting into authority to formulate or affect policy, particularly where the employee holds only \"basic analytical\" skills and the decision-makers are the VP and Product Development.")
B("**Sales support and data entry:** follow the Upsell Playbook and IT’s Data Quality Checklist; no discretion of the required kind.")
P("**Federal conclusion.** The CEAS likely fails both duties prongs: its primary duty is not administrative work, and even the minority analytics work, as written, does not clearly involve discretion and independent judgment on matters of significance. We assess the probability that an exempt classification would be sustained in litigation as low. Because the role is staffed by 18 employees performing identical duties under a single job description, it would also be a natural candidate for conditional certification of a collective action under 29 U.S.C. § 216(b).", "j")

H(1, "VI. State-Law Analysis")
H(2, "A. California — Irvine (6 Positions): Non-Exempt as a Matter of Law")
P("**1. Salary.** An exempt administrative employee in California must earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment. Cal. Lab. Code § 515(a); IWC Wage Order 4-2001 § 1(A)(2)(g). With the 2025 statewide minimum wage of $16.50/hour, the floor is $68,640 per year ($5,720 per month; $1,320 per week). The CEAS salary of $55,200 is **$13,440 (19.6%) short**. The Grade 7 maximum of $62,000 is also short. Because the threshold is pegged to the minimum wage, it rises every January 1 (the Department of Industrial Relations announces the annual CPI adjustment in the prior summer), so any future exempt California position must be re-tested annually — exactly as the 2022 audit warned (\"An employee earning $54,000 or $55,000 annually ... would fall short of California’s exempt salary threshold\"). Thornbury did not analyze California at all and disclaimed state law; the grid’s California note for the CEAS row is blank. Mr. Polk’s March 17 statement that he \"trust[s] they’ve done their diligence on the geographic piece\" is contradicted by the letter itself.", "j")
P("**2. Duties — \"primarily engaged.\"** California requires that the employee be \"primarily engaged\" in exempt duties, meaning more than one-half of work time. Cal. Lab. Code § 515(e); Wage Order 4-2001 § 1(A)(2)(f), § 2. The test is quantitative and is measured by the employer’s realistic expectations and the work actually performed. __Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co.__, 20 Cal. 4th 785 (1999). The Wage Order incorporates specified federal regulations (29 C.F.R. §§ 541.201–.205, .207–.208, .210, .215 as in effect in 2001) to define administrative work, but California does not adopt the federal flexible \"primary duty\" approach. See also __Harris v. Superior Court__, 53 Cal. 4th 170 (2011) (administrative/production dichotomy is not a dispositive test; analysis follows the Wage Order and incorporated regulations). With at most 25% arguably exempt time, the role fails by a wide margin.", "j")
P("**3. Consequences.** Irvine CEAS employees must receive daily overtime (1.5× after 8 hours/day and for the first 8 hours on the seventh consecutive day; 2× after 12 hours/day and after 8 on the seventh day), weekly overtime after 40, Cal. Lab. Code § 510; compliant meal periods (§ 512) and rest periods (Wage Order 4 § 12), with one hour of premium pay per day for each type of violation (§ 226.7); itemized wage statements showing hours and rates (§ 226); timely final pay (§§ 201–203). If a salaried-non-exempt structure is used, the salary is deemed to compensate only 40 hours and the regular rate is 1/40 of the weekly salary, § 515(d); the fluctuating-workweek method is not permitted in California. Misclassification exposure includes three-year Labor Code limitations (four years under Bus. & Prof. Code § 17208 for restitution), waiting-time penalties up to 30 days’ wages (§ 203), wage-statement penalties (§ 226(e)), and PAGA penalties (Lab. Code § 2699, as amended effective 2024, which reduces penalties for employers that take reasonable pre-notice compliance steps — another reason to fix this before hire).", "j")
H(2, "B. Oregon — Portland Remote Hub (4 Positions): Non-Exempt")
P("Oregon exempts bona fide executive, administrative and professional employees who meet the duties tests of the federal regulations and are paid a salary of at least the applicable Oregon minimum wage × 2,080 hours. ORS 653.020(3); OAR 839-020-0300(1)–(3). For the Portland metro region the minimum wage was $15.95/hour as of July 1, 2024 (annual floor $33,176), increasing to $16.30 on July 1, 2025 ($33,904); the CEAS salary clears this. The duties analysis, however, follows the federal regulations, and the role fails it for the reasons in Section V. Oregon employees must therefore receive overtime after 40 hours (ORS 653.261; OAR 839-020-0030), Oregon-compliant meal and rest periods (OAR 839-020-0050), and accurate itemized statements. Misclassification exposure includes unpaid overtime, statutory penalty wages of up to 30 days (ORS 652.150), civil penalties under ORS 653.055, and attorney fees. Because these employees work from home, the Company should confirm that each employee’s home is within the Portland metro boundary (which determines the applicable minimum-wage tier) and that remote timekeeping is in place.", "j")
H(2, "C. Texas — Austin (8 Positions)")
P("Texas has no state overtime statute; the Texas Minimum Wage Act defers to the FLSA for covered employers, Tex. Lab. Code ch. 62, and the Texas Payday Law governs pay timing. The federal analysis controls for Austin. Austin employees are within the Fifth Circuit, which has permitted the half-time (fluctuating workweek) method to compute damages for misclassified salaried employees in some circumstances (__Blackmon v. Brookshire Grocery Co.__, 835 F.2d 1135 (5th Cir. 1988)); this may reduce but does not eliminate exposure, and it is not a basis for classification.", "j")
